title: Om is the bow
hookLine: Angiras turns meditation into archery: om the bow, the self the arrow, Brahman the target
carry: om the bow, the self the arrow
tomorrow: the two birds on one tree
last: EVERY BEING IS A SPARK OF THE ONE FIRE.

lines: THINK OF DINNER, AND YOU MISS.
THE MUNDAKA HANDS YOU A BOW.
cards: Watch an archer just before the release. The whole body goes still. The breath slows, then stops.
The eyes stop darting. For one second there's nothing in the world but the line from the arrowhead to the mark. Let the mind drift to dinner, and the arrow drifts with it.
So when the Mundaka wants to describe meditation, it doesn't reach for a cushion or a mountain cave. It hands you a bow.

teach.b: Angiras does it in two verses. The first: take the great weapon of the Upanishad as your bow. Fit to it an arrow sharpened by meditation.
Draw it back with a mind absorbed in that, and hit the target, dear one: the imperishable. Then the second verse spells out the picture. Pranavo dhanuh: om is the bow.

teach.h: OM THE BOW, THE SELF THE ARROW.
teach.b: Sharo hy atma: the self is the arrow.
Brahma tal lakshyam uchyate: Brahman is called the target. Then two instructions. It must be struck by one who isn't careless, apramatta, undistracted.

teach.h: LIKE THE ARROW, BECOME ONE WITH IT.
teach.b: Like the arrow, become one with it. When an arrow hits its mark, it doesn't stay separate, hovering an inch away. It goes in.
It becomes part of the target.

Tanmaya means made of that, full of that, absorbed in it. You met that -maya, made of, a few weeks ago in the Taittiriya: the self made of food, of breath, of mind. Now the text asks you to become tan-maya, made of that.
Why is om the bow? Teachers explain that the sound, chanted or held in the mind, gathers attention and sends it. It's one reason so many Hindu prayers, pujas and classes begin with om.

And when the mind wanders mid-chant, many teachers say: no blame, just draw the bow again. The next verse adds: know the one self alone, in which sky and earth and mind are woven. This is the bridge to the deathless.
And then a blessing: may you cross safely to the far shore, beyond darkness.

how: Hindus who meditate with om chant it aloud or hold it in the mind, and some teachers use the Mundaka's bow and arrow to describe how the sound gathers attention toward one point.

o: the self, flying straight to its mark
Brahman, the target the archer aims at
om, which sends the self toward Brahman

games.q: the archer's picture — tap the pairs.

s: in the Mundaka, the arrow is om
om is the bow. the self is the arrow, and Brahman the target.
tanmaya means 'made of that, absorbed in it'
like the arrow in its mark, become one with it.
the text says the target must be struck by one who isn't careless

games.q: the arrow hits the mark. in the Mundaka's picture, what's the archer told to do?
o: pull the arrow back out and shoot again.
like the arrow, become one with it.
admire the shot from a distance.
games.why: sharavat tanmayo bhavet: like the arrow, become one with it. the arrow doesn't hover beside the mark; it goes in.

practice: Sit tall, like a drawn bow, and let a soft om come out on the breath, or simply hear it inside, gathering your attention the way a bow gathers its pull. Let the attention fly to one point, the stillness after the sound.
When the mind wanders, and it will, notice it without blame, and draw the bow again.

wordCard.voice: The bow. In the Mundaka, om is the bow, the self is the arrow, Brahman is the target, and the archer becomes one with it, like the arrow in the mark.

orig.note: Sanskrit tanmaya: tat, that, + maya, made of. 'like the arrow, become one with it', Mundaka 2.2.4.
